### WHAT IT IS
The **Compulsory Registration of Religious Conversions Bill, 2005** is a Private Member's Bill introduced by Shri Kashiram Rana in the Lok Sabha [1]. It seeks to mandate the pre-notification and statutory registration of all voluntary religious conversions across India to generate official conversion records for census and research purposes, while providing individuals a cooling-off period to exercise free will [2].

---

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor:** Shri Kashiram Rana, M.P. [1]
* **Instrument Type:** Private Member's Bill (Statutory Proposal) [1]
* **Stage & Status:** Introduced in Lok Sabha (2005); **Not in record** as enacted into law [1].
* **Territorial Extent:** Extends to the whole of India, coming into force in notified areas within one year of official publication [1].

---

### DESIGN: PRE-CONVERSION PROCEDURE
Under **Section 5** and **Section 7** of the Bill, any individual proposing to change their faith must adhere to the following steps:

1. **Preparation and Submission of Memorandum:**
   * The person must prepare and sign a memorandum in the prescribed form [3].
   * The memorandum must also be signed by the officiating priest, the head of the religious institution, or the person authorised to perform the ceremony [3].
   * It must be delivered or sent by registered post in triplicate to the local Registrar of Conversions **60 days before** the proposed conversion date [3].
   * A fee of **₹5** must accompany the memorandum [3].
2. **Statutory Notice & Transmission:**
   * The Registrar sends the third copy within **15 days** of receipt to the religious head, chief priest, community organisation, social body, or recognised mission of the faith from which the person proposes to convert [4].
3. **Conversion Window:**
   * Upon expiry of the **60-day notice period**, the person is entitled to effect the conversion, which must be completed within **45 days** thereafter [5].
4. **Post-Conversion Intimation:**
   * Following the ceremony, the converted person must deliver or send by registered post an intimation of conversion signed by himself, the officiating priest, and **three witnesses** to the Registrar to obtain a certificate of conversion [6].

---

### CONSEQUENCES IF THE PROCEDURE IS NOT FOLLOWED

| Area of Impact | Legal Consequence Under the Bill |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Validity of Conversion** | **Not Invalid Solely for Non-Registration:** Under **Section 9**, no conversion is invalid solely because it was not registered, or because the memorandum/intimation was not delivered, or was defective, irregular, or incorrect [7]. |
| **Government Benefits & Rights** | **Disqualification / Non-Recognition:** Under the proviso to **Section 9**, an unregistered conversion cannot be accepted as proof for any Central or State Government service. The individual is disentitled from any benefits, reservation, special privileges, rights, or scholarships granted by the government to that particular religion unless a certified copy of conversion is produced [8]. |
| **Penalties on Individual** | Under **Section 10**, anyone who willfully avoids or neglects to send/deliver the memorandum (Section 5) or intimation (Section 7), or makes materially false statements, is punishable on conviction with a fine up to **₹200** [9]. |
| **Penalties on Registrar** | Under **Section 11**, any Registrar who fails to file the memorandum (Section 6) or intimation (Section 7) faces rigorous imprisonment up to **3 months**, a fine up to **₹500**, or both [9]. |

---

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Evidentiary Thresholds:** Verification of whether proof of conversion is mandated by state executive departments for affirmative action or social welfare schemes [8].
* **Subsequent Legislative Tracking:** Private Member proposals of this nature rarely pass into statutory law; monitor state anti-conversion enactments where pre-conversion notice requirements (such as 30-to-60-day declarations to District Magistrates) have instead been codified by state legislatures.

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Compulsory Registration of Religious Conversions Bill, 2005** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in Parliament by **Shri Kashiram Rana, M.P.** [1]. The Bill establishes a statutory regime requiring individuals intending to alter or change their religion of birth or customary faith to register such conversion with designated state authorities [2, 3].

---

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor / Ownership:** Private Member's Bill introduced by **Shri Kashiram Rana, M.P.** [1].
* **Status / Stage:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha (Bill No. and detailed stage not specified beyond introduction text; not enacted into law) [1].
* **Territorial Extent:** Extends to the whole of India [1].
* **Commencement:** Section 1 was designed to come into force at once, while remaining provisions were to take effect within one year from publication in the Official Gazette on dates appointed by the Central Government for different areas [1].

---

### 3. DESIGN: PROCEDURES & CONSEQUENCES

#### What a Person Must Do Before Converting
1. **Prepare and Sign a Memorandum:** Under **Section 5(1)**, every person proposing to change or alter their religion of birth, customary faith, or religious practice of their own free will and voluntary choice must prepare and sign a memorandum in the form prescribed by the Central Government [3].
2. **Priest / Authority Signature:** Under **Section 5(2)**, the memorandum must also be signed by the officiating priest, head of the religious institution, or person authorized to perform the ceremony or rites at the time, date, and place specified [3].
3. **Deliver Triplicate Copies 60 Days in Advance:** The person must deliver or send by registered post the memorandum in triplicate to the local Registrar of Conversions **60 days before** the proposed date of conversion [3].
4. **Pay Fee:** The memorandum must be accompanied by a fee of **₹5** [3].
5. **Post-Notice Waiting Window:** Under **Section 7(1)**, only after the expiry of the **60-day** period is the person entitled to effect the conversion, which must then be completed within **45 days** from the expiry of the 60-day period [4].
6. **Post-Conversion Intimation:** Following the conversion, under **Section 7(2)**, the converted person must deliver or send by registered post to the Registrar an intimation of conversion signed by themselves, the officiating priest, and **three witnesses** [5].

#### What Happens If the Procedure Is Not Followed
* **Validity of the Conversion:** Under **Section 9**, a conversion is **not invalid solely** by reason of the fact that it was not registered, that the memorandum/intimation was not sent/delivered, or that it was defective, irregular, or incorrect [6].
* **Loss of State Benefits and Recognition:** Under the proviso to **Section 9**, an unregistered conversion cannot be accepted as proof for any service under the Central or State Government, and the converted person is **not entitled to any benefits, reservations, special privileges, rights, scholarships**, or other government benefits applicable to that new religion unless a certified copy of the conversion is produced [7].
* **Penal Consequences for the Individual:** Under **Section 10**, any person who willfully avoids or neglects to deliver/send the memorandum under Section 5 or intimation under Section 7, or who makes any statement false in any material particular knowing or believing it to be false, is punishable upon conviction with a **fine extending up to ₹200** [8].
* **Penal Consequences for Registrars:** Under **Section 11**, any Registrar who fails to file the memorandum under Section 6 or intimation under Section 7 is punishable upon conviction with **rigorous imprisonment up to 3 months**, a **fine extending up to ₹500**, or both [8].

---

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For (from the Statement of Objects and Reasons):** The Bill creates official records and statistics for census, research, and social work; ensures an individual has sufficient time (a mandatory cooling-off/notice window) to exercise free will; and seeks to curb alleged mass-scale conversions driven by inducement or compulsion that provoke communal conflict [2, 9].
* **Case Against / Concerns:** Imposes administrative delays (a 60-day pre-notification and external disclosures to heads of the religion being left under Section 6(4)), criminalizes procedural non-compliance with fines, and disqualifies individuals from statutory and state welfare benefits without registration [3, 7, 8, 10].

---

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Notification Mechanism:** Section 6(4) mandates transmitting the memorandum within 15 days to the religious head, chief priest, community organization, or social body of the religion the person is leaving, creating direct institutional exposure [10].
* **Certification Registry:** Verification of conversions strictly depends on extracts from the official Register of Conversions issued under Section 8 (on payment of ₹2) to access public reservations or benefits [6, 7].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Compulsory Registration of Religious Conversions Bill, 2005** is a Private Member's Bill introduced by Shri Kashiram Rana in Parliament to mandate the statutory registration of all voluntary religious conversions across India [2][3]. It establishes a formal notice, verification, and certification mechanism to record conversions and prevent disputes surrounding forced conversions or enticements [1][13].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor / Ministry:** Introduced by **Shri Kashiram Rana, M.P.** [2] (Administrative ownership would lie with the Central Government via appointed Registrars and Registrars-General [19]).
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory proposal (Private Member's Bill) [2].
* **Status / Stage:** Introduced in 2005; not enacted into law [2].

### DESIGN: PRE-CONVERSION REQUIREMENTS & CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE

#### What a Person Must Do Before Converting
Under Clause 5 and Clause 7 of the Bill, any individual intending to convert must undertake the following steps:
1. **Prepare a Memorandum:** Every person seeking to change their religion of birth or customary faith voluntarily and of their own free will must prepare and sign a memorandum in the form prescribed by the Central Government [3].
2. **Priest's Signature:** The memorandum must also be signed by the officiating priest, head of the religious institution, or person authorised to perform the ceremony or rites, specifying the date, time, and place of the proposed ceremony [3].
3. **Deliver in Triplicate:** The memorandum must be delivered or sent by registered post in triplicate to the local area Registrar **60 days before** the date of the proposed conversion [3].
4. **Fee Payment:** The memorandum must be accompanied by a fee of **₹5** [3].
5. **Observe the Waiting Period & Timeline:** The person must wait for the expiry of the 60-day notice period before effecting the conversion, after which the conversion must be completed within **45 days** from the date the 60-day period expires [5].
6. **Post-Conversion Intimation:** After the ceremony, the converted individual must deliver or send by registered post an intimation of conversion to the Registrar, signed by themselves, the officiating priest, and **three witnesses** [7].

#### What Happens if the Procedure Is Not Followed
Under Clauses 9, 10, and 11, the consequences of failing to follow the procedure include:

* **Validity of the Conversion Remains Intact:** Under Clause 9, no conversion is invalid solely because it was not registered, or because the memorandum/intimation was not delivered/sent, or because the documentation was defective, irregular, or incorrect [20].
* **Loss of Government Benefits and Privileges:** Under the proviso to Clause 9, an unregistered conversion **shall not be accepted as proof** for any service under the Central or State Government, nor will it entitle the person to any benefits, reservations, special privileges, rights, scholarships, or concessions accorded by the Central or State Government to persons of that particular religion, unless a certified copy of conversion is produced [12].
* **Penalties for Individuals:** Under Clause 10, any person who wilfully avoids or neglects to send/deliver the memorandum (under Clause 5) or the intimation (under Clause 7), or who knowingly makes a materially false statement in them, is liable on conviction to a fine of up to **₹200** [6].
* **Penalties for Registrars:** Under Clause 11, any Registrar who fails to file the memorandum or the intimation of conversion is punishable on conviction with rigorous imprisonment of up to **three months**, or a fine of up to **₹500**, or both [6].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Standardises public statistical records for census, social work, and demographic research while providing individuals a mandatory cooling-off window (60 days) to ensure decisions are voluntary and free from coercion or enticement [1][13].
* **Case Against:** Creates bureaucratic hurdles, administrative surveillance, and notice requirements (including forwarding copies of the memorandum to local community bodies of the originating religion), potentially chilling the fundamental right to freedom of conscience [11][18].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Tracking Enactment & State Legislation:** The Bill was not passed; track state-level "Freedom of Religion" statutes, which routinely incorporate prior-notice requirements (30 to 60 days) to District Magistrates rather than a Central registration framework.

### WHAT IT IS

The **Compulsory Registration of Religious Conversions Bill, 2005** is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri Kashiram Rana [1], [2]. It provides a statutory mechanism requiring compulsory prior notice, registration, and post-ceremony intimation of all voluntary religious conversions in India to establish public statistics and prevent conversions under compulsion or inducement [1], [3].

---

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS

| Parameter | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Sponsor / Ownership** | Shri Kashiram Rana, M.P. (Private Member's Bill) [1] |
| **Statutory Status** | As-introduced Bill (not enacted into law) [1] |
| **Jurisdiction** | Extends to the whole of India [1] |
| **Central Machinery** | Central Government-appointed Registrar-General and local Registrars of Conversions [4] |

---

### DESIGN: PRE-CONVERSION REQUIREMENTS & CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE

#### 1. What a Person Must Do Before Converting

Under **Clause 5** and **Clause 7** of the Bill, any person intending to alter or change their religion of birth or faith must follow a strict pre-conversion timeline and procedural protocol [2], [5]:

* **Eligibility**: The person must have completed the age of **18 years** and act of their own will and voluntary choice [2], [6].
* **Prepare and Sign a Memorandum**: The person must prepare and sign a memorandum of conversion in the prescribed form [2].
* **Co-Signatures**: The memorandum must also be signed by the officiating priest, the head of the religious institution, or the person authorised to perform the rites/ceremony at the specified time, date, and place [2].
* **Advance Delivery**: The memorandum must be delivered or sent by registered post in **triplicate** to the local Registrar of Conversions **60 days before** the proposed conversion date [2].
* **Statutory Fee**: The memorandum must be accompanied by a fee of **₹5** [2].
* **Waiting Period & Execution Window**: The individual must wait until the **60-day period expires**. Upon expiry, they are entitled to effect the conversion, which must be completed within **45 days** from the expiration of the 60-day notice period [5].

*(Post-conversion, the person must deliver an intimation of conversion signed by themselves, the officiating priest, and **three witnesses** to the Registrar to obtain a conversion certificate) [7].*

#### 2. What Happens if the Procedure Is Not Followed

If the mandated statutory procedure is omitted, neglected, or violated, the Bill outlines specific legal, civil, and penal consequences:

* **Validity of the Conversion (Clause 9)**: Non-registration or defective submission does **not invalidate** the religious conversion itself. No conversion is invalid solely because it was not registered, the memorandum/intimation was not delivered, or the filing was defective, irregular, or incorrect [8].
* **Forfeiture of State Benefits and Rights (Clause 9 Proviso)**: A conversion that is not registered and certified **shall not be accepted as proof** for any service under the Central or State Government, nor will it entitle the person to any benefits, reservations, special privileges, rights, scholarships, or concessions provided to members of that religion without producing a certified copy from the Register [8], [9].
* **Penalties on the Individual (Clause 10)**: Any person who willfully avoids or neglects to deliver or send the memorandum under Clause 5 or intimation under Clause 7, or makes any materially false statement knowing or believing it to be false, is liable on conviction to a **fine extending up to ₹200** [10].
* **Penalties on the Registrar (Clause 11)**: Any Registrar who fails to file the memorandum (pursuant to Clause 6) or intimation (pursuant to Clause 7) faces conviction with **rigorous imprisonment up to three months**, a **fine up to ₹500**, or both [10].

---

### TRADE-OFFS

* **Arguments for (from Bill Objects & Reasons)**: Provides credible statistical data for census and social research; institutes a mandatory 60-day cooling-off window ensuring individuals exercise free will rather than reacting under immediate duress, financial inducement, or communal conflict [3].
* **Arguments against (from Record & Bill Design)**: Imposes administrative hurdles, third-party disclosure requirements (notifying original faith leadership under Clause 6(4)), and bureaucratic state monitoring on individual religious freedom [11].

---

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH

* **Desk Status**: **Not in record** on whether this Private Member's Bill progressed beyond the introduction stage in Lok Sabha before lapsing.
* **Key Administrative Chokepoints**: Appointment of local Registrars, Central notification of faith organizations under Clause 6(4) / 14(3), and institutional capacity to manage registries [4], [11], [12].

### WHAT IT IS The Coinage Bill, 2011 (enacted as the Coinage Act, 2011) consolidates the laws relating to coinage and the Government Mints, protects legal tender coinage, and establishes strict prohibitions and penal sanctions against the unlawful making, possession, importation, melting, or destruction of coins [1]. ### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS * **Administrative Ownership:** Central Government (Ministry of Finance / Government Mints / Reserve Bank of India) [1, 2]. * **Legal Instrument:** Statutory legislation (enacted as Act No. 11 of 2011, receiving Presidential assent on **1 September 2011**) [1]. * **Procedural Classification:** Under Section 19, offences under the Act are **cognizable** and **bailable**, but **non-compoundable** [3]. Under Section 21, offences may be tried summarily by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or a Metropolitan Magistrate [3]. Section 18 bars the application of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 [4]. ### OFFENCES, CONDUCT, AND PENALTIES Chapter V and Chapter VI specify the following penal provisions: | Provision | Prohibited Conduct | Prescribed Penalty | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Section 12 read with Section 13** | • Using any metal piece as coin (stamped or unstamped) intended for use as money, except by Government authority [5].

• Using coins other than as a medium of exchange [5].
• Having possession, custody, or control of melted coin (molten or solid), destroyed/mutilated coin, or coins substantially in excess of reasonable requirements for selling above face value, melting, destroying, or disposing other than as a medium of exchange [5]. | **Imprisonment extending up to 7 years and with fine** [2]. | | **Section 14(1) read with Section 14(2)** | • Making, issuing, or attempting to issue any metal piece as coin (except under Section 4) [2].

Section 12(3) explicitly exempts authorized Mint disposals/auctions, the RBI, authorized coin blank suppliers, and prospective tender sample suppliers [2]. ### TRADE-OFFS * **Case For:** Provides deterrent criminal penalties (up to seven years of imprisonment) to curb illicit syndicates melting metallic currency for metal scrap value or issuing unauthorized tokens as parallel money [2, 5]. * **Case Against:** The statutory presumption against possession of matching alloys and broad tests for "excess of reasonable requirements" create compliance exposure for commercial scrap handlers and bulk cash handlers [5, 6]. ### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH * **Enforcement Tracking:** Monitor police registration under Section 19 (cognizable/bailable) and summary trial disposal rates under Judicial and Metropolitan Magistrates [3]. * **Forfeiture Execution:** Track Government confiscation proceedings under Section 17 for seized consignments at ports or scrap units [4].

### Clarification on Section 39 As shown in the statutory text of the Coinage Act, 2011, the enactment contains **28 sections** in total [1, 7, 12]. The reference to "section 39" in section 20 of the Act is an amendment to **Section 39 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934** (substituting "the Coinage Act, 2011" in place of "the Indian Coinage Act, 1906"), rather than a penalty section of the Coinage Bill/Act itself [37]. It is therefore not a penal provision of the Coinage Bill, 2011. --- ### WHAT IT IS The Coinage Bill, 2011 (enacted as the Coinage Act, 2011) consolidates the laws relating to coinage and the Mints, protects legal tender coinage, and prohibits the melting, destruction, unauthorized possession, or unauthorized making/issue of coins and coinage metal in India [1]. ### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS * **Authority**: Central Government [1, 51]. * **Status**: Act of Parliament (Act No. 11 of 2011), assented to by the President on **1st September, 2011** [1]. * **Offence Classification & Procedure**: Offences under the Act are **cognizable** and **bailable**, but **non-compoundable** [37]. *(A statutory presumption of contravention applies if found possessing metal/material containing alloys in the same proportions used in coin manufacture, unless proved otherwise [8]; exceptions apply to mint auction scraps, the Mint, RBI and agents, or bona fide tender sample suppliers [2]).* | Imprisonment extending up to **7 years** and with **fine** [2]. | | **Section 14(1) read with Section 14(2)** [3] | • Making, issuing, or attempting to issue any metal piece as coin (except authorized minting under Section 4) [3].
• Possessing, holding custody, or control of any metal piece with intent to issue it for use as money as a medium of exchange [3]. | • **First offence**: Imprisonment extending up to **1 year**, or with **fine**, or with **both** [3].
• **Subsequent conviction**: Imprisonment extending up to **3 years**, or with **fine**, or with **both** [3]. | | **Section 15(1) read with Section 15(2)** [3] | Bringing into India by sea, land, or air any piece of metal to be used as coin without Government authority or permission [3]. | Imprisonment extending up to **7 years** and with **fine** [3]. | | **Section 17** [45] | Any coin or metal involved in an offence under the Act [45]. | **Forfeiture** of such coin or metal to the Government [45]. | ### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH * **Statutory Presumption & Defences**: Enforcement targets scrap dealers and individuals possessing metal alloy matches under Section 12(2), who must demonstrate auction provenance or standard business requirements [2, 8]. * **Trial Scrutiny**: Summary jurisdiction applied by Magistrates under Section 21 [37].

### WHAT IT IS The Coinage Bill, 2011 (enacted as the Coinage Act, 2011) consolidates and amends the laws governing coinage, Mints, and the protection of legal currency in India [1]. Chapter V of the Act defines specific criminal offences and prescribes severe penalties—including up to seven years of imprisonment—to prohibit the unlawful making, possession, importation, melting, destruction, and non-monetary exploitation of coins [2, 3, 5]. --- ### PENALTIES AND PROHIBITED CONDUCT | Provision | Prohibited Conduct | Prescribed Penalties | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Section 12 read with Section 13** [2, 5] | **Melting, destruction, and unauthorized use of coins:**
• Using any metal piece as a coin (stamped or unstamped) intended for use as money without Central Government authority [5];
• Melting or destroying any coin [5];
• Using coins other than as a medium of exchange [5];
• Possessing, keeping custody of, or controlling:
  – any melted coin, whether in a molten or solid state [5];
  – any coin in a destroyed or mutilated state [5];
  – coins substantially in excess of reasonable requirements to sell them at other than face value, melt, destroy, or dispose of them other than as a medium of exchange [5]. | **Imprisonment up to 7 years and fine** [2]. | | **Section 14(1) read with Section 14(2)** [3] | **Unauthorized making, issuing, or possession for issue:**
• Making, issuing, or attempting to issue any metal piece for use as coin, except as authorized under Section 4 (which allows minting by the Government at Mints or authorized facilities up to ₹1,000 denominations) [3, 41];
• Having possession, custody, or control of any metal piece with the intent to issue it for use as money or a medium of exchange [3]. | **First Conviction:** Imprisonment up to **1 year, or fine, or both** [3].
**Subsequent Conviction:** Imprisonment up to **3 years, or fine, or both** [3]. | | **Section 15(1) read with Section 15(2)** [3] | **Unlawful import of metal pieces for coinage:**
• Bringing into India by sea, land, or air any piece of metal to be used as coin without the authority or permission of the Central Government [3]. | **Imprisonment up to 7 years and fine** [3]. | --- ### STATUTORY PRESUMPTIONS, EXEMPTIONS & PROCEDURE * **Presumption of Guilt (Section 12(2)):** Anyone found in possession of metal or material containing alloys in the identical proportions used in the manufacture of any coin is presumed, until proven otherwise, to have contravened Section 12(1) [8]. * **Statutory Exceptions (Section 12(3)):** Section 12 does not apply to [2]: 1. Possession of non-recyclable coinage metal scrap or scissel obtained through lawful Mint auction disposals [2]; 2. The Mint, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), authorized agents, and suppliers fulfilling official Government orders [2]; 3. Prospective suppliers holding reasonable quantities of sample coins/blanks pursuant to valid tender documents [2]. * **Procedural Classification (Section 19 & Section 21):** Offences under the Act are **cognizable and bailable, but not compoundable** [37]. They may be tried summarily by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or a Metropolitan Magistrate [37].

### WHAT IT IS The Coinage Bill, 2011 (enacted as the Coinage Act, 2011) consolidates the laws relating to coinage and the Mints, the protection of coinage, and explicitly prohibits the melting, destruction, unauthorised making, possession, and unlawful import of coins and metal pieces intended for use as money [1]. ### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS * **Ministry:** Ministry of Finance (Central Government) [1, 46]. * **Status:** Enacted statutory legislation; received Presidential assent on **1st September, 2011** [1]. * **Procedural Nature:** Offences under the Act are cognizable and bailable, but not compoundable, and may be tried summarily by a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class or a Metropolitan Magistrate [37]. ### PENALTIES AND PROHIBITED CONDUCT Chapter V of the Act sets out three distinct sets of penalties and prohibited conduct: | Section | Prohibited Conduct | Prescribed Penalty | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Section 12 contraventions (punishable under Section 13)** [2, 5] | • Using any metal piece as a coin intended to be used as money except by Government authority [5];
• Melting or destroying any coin [5];
• Using coin other than as a medium of exchange [5];
• Having possession, custody, or control of: (a) any melted coin (molten or solid state), (b) any destroyed or mutilated coin, or (c) coins substantially in excess of reasonable requirements for selling above face value, melting, destroying, or disposing of other than as a medium of exchange [5]. | **Imprisonment up to 7 years and with fine** [2]. | | **Section 14(1) contraventions (punishable under Section 14(2))** [3] | • Making, issuing, or attempting to issue any metal piece for the purpose of a coin (except as provided under Section 4) [3];
• Having possession, custody, or control of any metal piece with the intent to issue it for use as money for a medium of exchange [3]. | **First conviction:** Imprisonment up to 1 year, or with fine, or with both [3].
**Subsequent conviction:** Imprisonment up to 3 years, or with fine, or with both [3]. | | **Section 15(1) contraventions (punishable under Section 15(2))** [3] | • Bringing by sea, land, or air into India any piece of metal to be used as coin except with the authority or permission of the Government [3]. | **Imprisonment up to 7 years and with fine** [3]. | ### STATUTORY PRESUMPTION AND EXCEPTIONS * **Presumption:** Anyone found in possession of metal or material containing alloys in the same proportions as used in coin manufacture is presumed, until the contrary is proved, to have contravened Section 12(1) [8]. * **Exemptions from Section 12:** Section 12 does not apply to: (i) persons possessing non-recyclable coinage metal scrap or scissel acquired via valid Mint auctions; (ii) the Mint, RBI, their authorised agents, and contracted suppliers/coin-blank suppliers; and (iii) prospective suppliers holding reasonable sample quantities against valid tender documents [2, 8]. ### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH * **Enforcement Criteria:** Track enforcement standards under the Explanation to Section 12(1) assessing "reasonable requirements" based on daily coin needs, profession, mode of acquisition, and holding location [8]. * **Summary Trials:** Monitor execution by Judicial Magistrates of the First Class or Metropolitan Magistrates under Section 21 [37].

### WHAT IT IS The **Senior Citizens (Welfare) Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri Chandrakant Khaire, M.P. [1]. It establishes a statutory framework to provide social security—comprising regular monthly pensions, medical care, and residential facilities—to destitute older persons, administered via a three-tier board and committee structure, while making it a legally enforceable duty for individuals to maintain their aged parents and grandparents under threat of criminal penalties [1, 2, 3]. ### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS * **Sponsoring Authority:** Private Member's Bill introduced by Shri Chandrakant Khaire, M.P. [1]. * **Nodal Department & Board Leadership:** Nodal oversight is vested in the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment; the Secretary of the Ministry serves as the ex officio Chairman of the Central Board for Senior Citizens' Welfare [1]. * **Statutory Status:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha during 2001 (52nd Year of the Republic of India) [1]. * **Arguments from the Record:** Rapid socio-economic shifts leave elderly persons without family support or independent livelihood, necessitating statutory social security, healthcare, and dignified shelter from the welfare state [3, 8].

### 3. DESIGN

#### How a Woman Obtains Protection
* **Reporting Domestic Violence:** Any person having reason to believe an act of domestic violence has been, is being, or is likely to be committed may report it to the Protection Officer [7]. Informants acting in good faith incur no civil or criminal liability under Section 8(2) [7].
* **Presentation of Application:** Under Section 9(1), an application seeking relief under Section 14 may be presented to the Magistrate by:
  1. The aggrieved person herself [7];
  2. Any other person on her behalf [7]; or
  3. The Protection Officer [7].
* **Jurisdiction:** The Judicial Magistrate of the first class or the Metropolitan Magistrate exercising jurisdiction in the area where the aggrieved person resides [4].

Under Section 15(1), the protection order remains in force in the first instance for a period fixed by the Magistrate, **not exceeding two years** [8]. Copies are forwarded to the Protection Officer and the parties [8].

#### What Happens If the Order Is Breached
* **Penal Consequences:** Under the main features of the 2002 Bill, violation by the relative of an order made by the Magistrate constitutes an offence punishable with **imprisonment up to one year, or with fine, or with both** [9].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS

The **Public Liability Insurance (Amendment) Bill, 1992** amends the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 to resolve an operational impasse that occurred when insurers refused to underwrite policies covering unlimited owner liability [2, 6]. The Bill caps an insurer's liability to the contracted insurance amount while leaving the owner's liability unlimited, fixes statutory floors and ceilings for required coverage, mandates owner contributions to an Environmental Relief Fund, and expands the statutory definitions of "owner" and "accident" [2, 6, 16, 19, 46].

* **Administrative Ministry**: Ministry of Environment and Forests (introduced by Minister of State Kamal Nath) [3, 7].

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition of "Owner"** | A person who has control over handling any hazardous substance [4]. | Expanded to any person who *owns* or has control over handling at the time of the accident; explicitly includes partners in a firm, members of an association, and directors, managers, secretaries, or officers directly in charge of and responsible for the company's business conduct [16]. |
| **Definition of "Accident"** | An accident or incident occurring while handling any hazardous substance [4]. | Modified to mean a fortuitous, sudden, or unintended occurrence resulting in continuous, intermittent, or repeated exposure causing death, injury, or property damage (excluding war or radio-activity) [2]. |
| **Insurance Policy Limits** | No statutory capital floor or ceiling prescribed in the statute [4, 6]. | A policy taken out or renewed cannot be less than the **paid-up capital** of the undertaking (defined for non-companies as the market value of all assets and stocks on the date of contract), and cannot exceed an amount prescribed by rules, up to a statutory cap of **₹50 crore** [19]. |

The **Public Liability Insurance (Amendment) Bill, 1992** amends the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 to resolve an impasse where insurers declined to issue policies covering unlimited owner liability [6]. While preserving the statutory principle of unlimited "no-fault" liability for owners who handle hazardous substances [1, 6], the Bill caps insurer liability under an insurance policy [6, 41], mandates owner contributions into a newly created **Environmental Relief Fund (ERF)** [6, 41, 46], defines policy cover limits pegged to paid-up capital [19], broadens the definition of an "owner" [16], and gives Collectors the power to issue injunctions against asset disposal by owners attempting to evade compensation awards [3, 46].

---

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry:** Ministry of Environment and Forests [3, 7, 17].
* **Instrument:** Statutory amendment bill (replacing the Public Liability Insurance (Amendment) Ordinance, 1992, promulgated on 31 January 1992) [1, 3].
* **Commencement:** Deemed to have come into force on **31 January 1992** [2].

---

### 3. DESIGN: SPECIFIC CHANGES FOR OWNERS

| Area | Prior Position under 1991 Act | Amendment Bill, 1992 Change |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition of "Owner"** | A person who has control over handling any hazardous substance [4]. | Expanded to include a person who *owns* or has control over handling hazardous substances at the time of the accident; specifically includes partners (in firms), members (in associations), and directors/managers/secretaries/officers directly in charge of company business [16]. |
| **Scope of "Accident"** | An accident or incident occurring while handling any hazardous substance [4]. | Explicitly requires a fortuitous, sudden, or unintended occurrence resulting in continuous, intermittent, or repeated exposure, excluding accidents caused only by war or radioactivity [2]. |
| **Policy Coverage Limits** | Unlimited liability without defined floor/ceiling parameters [6]. | Section 4(2A): Policies cannot be for less than the undertaking's paid-up capital (or market value of assets and stocks for non-companies), and cannot exceed a prescribed ceiling up to **₹50 crore** [19]. Insurer payout under a single policy is capped at the contracted sum [41]. |
| **Environmental Relief Fund (ERF) Contribution** | Not present in principal Act [16, 46]. | Section 4(2C): Owners must pay an additional sum alongside their insurance premium, not exceeding the premium amount itself, to be credited to the ERF established under Section 7A [41, 46]. |
| **Liability & Award Payments** | Insurers and owners paid under broad directions [4]. | Owner liability remains **unlimited** [6]. If the award exceeds the insurer's contracted limit, the balance is drawn from the ERF under the prescribed scheme, and any remaining amount awarded must be deposited by the owner as directed by the Collector [41, 43, 46]. |
| **Restraint on Asset Stripping** | Not explicitly provided under the award mechanism [3]. | Section 7(8): If an owner is likely to remove or dispose of property to evade award payments, the Collector may grant a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1–4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 [46]. |

---

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For:** Eliminates an unviable underwriting condition—unlimited insurer liability—which had completely stalled the implementation of mandatory public liability cover [6]. By establishing the ERF via matched owner contributions, it ensures an immediate interim liquidity pool for accident victims without diluting the owner's ultimate civil liability [6, 41, 46].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Imposes an increased immediate cash-flow cost on hazardous facility operators, who must pay up to an additional 100% of their policy premium into the ERF [41], while corporate officers and partners face direct statutory exposure under the tightened definition of "owner" [16].

---

* **Central ERF Scheme:** Promulgation of administrative schemes and statutory rules under Section 7A and Section 23 governing ERF remittance timetables, fund administration authorities, and maximum insurance policy limits [9, 11, 42].
* **Insurer Remittance:** Enforcement of Section 4(2D), under which failure by insurers to deposit ERF collections makes amounts recoverable as arrears of land revenue [41].
* **Collector Injunctions:** Exercise of civil court powers (Order XXXIX CPC) by district collectors against industrial asset transfers [46].

| Area | Prior Law (1991 Act) | Amended Requirement (1992 Bill) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition of "Owner"** | Defined strictly as a person who has control over handling any hazardous substance [6]. | Expanded to any person who **owns, or has control over handling**, hazardous substances at the time of an accident, expressly including partners in a firm, members in an association, and directors/managers/officers in charge of a company [7]. |

| **Environmental Relief Fund (ERF) Levy** | No dedicated relief fund mechanism [1]. | Every owner must pay to the insurer, alongside the premium, an additional prescribed contribution not exceeding the **sum equivalent to the premium**, to be credited to the ERF under section 7A [1, 8]. |

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The Communal Violence (Prevention, Control and Rehabilitation of Victims) Bill, 2005 (introduced in Parliament by Shri Ajit Singh, M.P.) is a legislative instrument designed to curb communal violence, fix public accountability, and statutorily mandate relief, employment, and monetary compensation for victims and their dependants [1, 2, 3]. It proposes establishing a five-member National Commission for Inter-Community Peace and Justice to determine claims and supervise compensation [1, 4, 5].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ownership & Auspices:** Private Member Bill sponsored by Shri Ajit Singh, M.P. [2]. Executive obligations are placed on the "appropriate Government" (the State Government in a State, and the Central Government in Union Territories or other cases) [2].
* **Statutory Status:** Introduced bill; it was not enacted into law [1, 2].

### 3. DESIGN: COMPENSATION & RELIEF PROVISIONS
The Bill establishes a multi-tiered compensation, employment, and adjudication framework:

* **Lumpsum Death Compensation (Clause 8):** The appropriate Government must pay a lumpsum compensation of **not less than ₹2 lakh** to the dependant(s) of any person killed in communal violence anywhere in the country [1, 6].
* **Employment Assistance (Clause 9):** If the deceased victim was the sole earning member of the family, the appropriate Government must provide suitable employment to at least one eligible and dependent member within **eight months** of the occurrence of violence [1, 6, 7].
* **Injury Compensation (Clause 10):** A person injured during communal violence is entitled to compensation paid by the appropriate Government as recommended by the National Commission for Inter-Community Peace and Justice [1, 7].
* **Adjudication of Claims & Additional Quantum (Clause 12):**
  * The Commission is empowered to invite claims from all persons entitled to compensation for loss of life, limb, serious injury, or property damage [4].
  * The Commission is authorised to decide additional compensation **over and above** the ₹2 lakh floor provided in Clause 8, as well as name the recipient(s) [1, 4].
* **Institutional Oversight (Clause 11):** Establishes the National Commission for Inter-Community Peace and Justice, consisting of a Chairman (a retired Supreme Court judge or retired High Court Chief Justice) and four members (a senior jurist eligible for the High Court bench, a retired Central Government Secretary, a retired Director General of Police, and a human rights activist with 20+ years of experience) [1, 5].
* **Right to Appeal (Clause 13):** Victims are granted the statutory right to appeal to civil courts against Commission decisions regarding compensation [4].
* **Definition of Dependants (Explanation to Clauses 8, 9, and 10):** Dependants eligible for relief include:
  1. A widow, minor legitimate or adopted son, unmarried legitimate or adopted daughter, or widowed mother [7];
  2. An infirm son or daughter who has attained 18 years of age, if wholly dependent on the deceased's earnings at death [7];
  3. A widower or a parent (other than a widowed mother), if wholly or partly dependent on the victim's earnings at the time of death or injury [7].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Merits in Design:** Sets an absolute statutory monetary floor (₹2 lakh) for deceased victims, enforces livelihood support via a time-bound public job guarantee (8 months), covers property and grievous injury losses, and opens access to ordinary civil courts on appeal [1, 4, 6, 7].
* **Administrative & Fiscal Burden:** The Financial Memorandum projects an annual recurring cost of ₹20 crore and non-recurring expenditure of ₹50 crore from the Consolidated Fund of India, alongside heavy fiscal and administrative obligations on State Governments to provide permanent public jobs within strict deadlines [1].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Adjudication Bottlenecks:** Dual jurisdiction between the National Commission determining loss of limb/property (Clause 12) and civil courts handling appeals (Clause 13) [4].
* **Job Delivery Monitoring:** Compliance by State Governments within the mandatory 8-month window under Clause 9 [6, 7].

### CONSEQUENCES IF CONDITIONS ARE NOT MET

If the conditions under Clause 4 are contravened, the Bill specifies distinct civil and penal outcomes depending on the violated condition:

* **Bigamy / Living Spouse (Contravention of Clause 4(ii))**:
  - **Nullity and Voidness**: Under **Clause 6**, any marriage solemnised in contravention of Clause 4(ii) is **null and void** and may, on a petition presented by either party against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity [9]. Under **Clause 19(1)**, such a marriage is expressly void [39].
  - **Criminal Prosecution**: The provisions of **Sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code** apply accordingly (Clause 19(1)) [39].

* **Underage Marriage (Contravention of Clause 4(iii))**:
  - **Penal Punishment**: Under **Clause 19(2)**, every person who procures a marriage of himself or herself to be solemnised in contravention of the age requirements specified in Clause 4(iii) is punishable with **simple imprisonment which may extend to fifteen days, or a fine of ₹1,000, or both** [3, 39].

* **Mental Incapacity / Infitness (Contravention of Clause 4(iv))**:
  - **Not in record.** (The retrieved Bill text does not specify an explicit separate penalty or nullity clause for contraventions of Clause 4(iv)).

* **Legitimacy of Children**:
  - Under **Clause 5**, notwithstanding that a marriage is null and void under the Bill, any child born of such marriage who would have been legitimate if the marriage had been valid is deemed **legitimate**, whether born before or after commencement, and whether or not a decree of nullity is granted or the marriage is held void otherwise than on a petition [9, 26].
